data.title: Consumer confidence dips in September amid inflation concerns
data.description:
U.S. consumer sentiment dipped to a four-month low in September amid rising inflation rates and mounting cost-of-living concerns, according to survey results released Friday.

The University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers‘ index found that consumer confidence slipped to a reading of 48.1 in September, a seven percent decrease from August and 15 percent less than in January

The measure uses how people feel about personal finances, as well as the broader economy, to predict future spending — which accounts for the bulk of U.S. economic activity.  

Consumer sentiment largely declined across the political spectrum, with both Republicans and Democrats confidence down from January. Republican sentiment in September is 20 percent lower than in January, while Democrats are down 13 percent over the same period, according to the survey.

Joanna Hsu, the director of the Surveys of Consumers, cited renewed worries over rising fuel prices and re-escalation of trade disputes as primary factors driving the downturn in American consumers’ confidence.

“Overall, interviews reveal broad agreement across demographic and political groups that the outlook for the economy has softened over the course of the year,” she said in a statement.

She also noted that, after declining for two months, the number of interviewees who spontaneously referenced gasoline when asked about the economy increased in September to 31 percent.

The effective shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz, through which 20 percent of the world’s oil is exported, has led to sharply rising gas and diesel prices as the U.S.’s war with Iran rages on. The national average for gas reached $4.49 per gallon as of Friday, $1.34 higher than last year’s average, according to AAA. Meanwhile, diesel’s price per gallon reached $6.50.

“In fact, consumers do not believe that relief from high gas prices is on the horizon; they broadly expect gasoline prices to continue rising in both the short and long run,” Hsu said.

An Emerson College poll found 60 percent of U.S. adults believe President Trump’s policies are making the economy worse. The number is higher compared to Emerson College’s 100 Day Poll from April 2025, in which 49 percent of respondents said Trump’s decisions had negatively impacted the economy.

The Michigan survey reported inflation expectations jumped from August to September, from 4 percent to 4.6 percent. The percentage also exceeds February’s reading of 3.4 percent, before the U.S. and Israel launched strikes against Iran, as well as expectations rates for all of 2024.

Long-run inflation expectations ticked up in September to 3.4 percent from three consecutive months at 3.3. These expectations are higher than 2024 readings, which ranged from 2.8 percent to 3.2 percent.

data.title: 5 takeaways from Trump and Xi's 'Made for TV' summit
data.description:
President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping concluded a lavish three-day summit in Washington, D.C., Friday, pledging to meet at least two more times this year. 

It was one of the few, solid commitments announced during the meetings, which saw other high-stakes issues fall to the background. This includes negotiations over Artificial Intelligence regulation, long-term trade agreements, Taiwan’s security and the release of Americans detained in China.

The president’s supporters describe Trump’s hosting of Xi as handling America’s chief adversary and toughest competitor responsibly – maintaining good, if not close relations and continuing the conversation.

But critics are outraged that Trump afforded the rare honor of a State visit to an authoritarian leader looking to usurp America’s position as the global leader and trample on democratic freedoms.

Here are five takeaways from Trump’s summit with Xi: 

On surface, more pomp and circumstance than substance

Xi’s arrival in the U.S. on Wednesday kicked off an extravagant three days of ceremonies. 

The president took the rare and unusual decision to meet Xi on the tarmac of Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, laying out a red carpet, bringing along an honor guard and experiencing the power of a B1 bomber flyover at low-altitude. 

Trump showed off his favorite things to Xi, the construction projects around the White House – the paved-over Rose Garden, the granite helicopter pad, the controversial ballroom. And he took an opportunity to disparage his predecessor, pointing out a framed photo of an autopen he says represents President Biden, among portraits of U.S. presidents. 

An opulent dinner capped off the events, with more than 100 invited guests including the titans of the tech world representing Amazon, Nvidia, X and others. 

Trump largely shielded Xi from the press, a noticeable departure from the president’s freewheeling Oval Office meetings with other heads of state.

Xi tightly controls speech in his country, jailing political opponents or any perceived enemies, including U.S. citizens. He’s accused of carrying out a campaign of genocide against the Uyghur Muslim minority. 

“Everything has been done to the highest order of perfection and there’s thought in every little detail, and it’s greatly appreciated,” Xi said during tea with Trump and their wives, as an instrumental version of “Stand By Me” played serenely in the background.

Press were ushered out at the conclusion of the remarks.

On trade, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Wednesday before the summit began that the U.S. and China had agreed to extend their trade truce for two months. He told Fox News’ Bret Baier that the extension is to “give us more time to see what we can do on the economic front.”

Nothing more on that note was announced.

Anti-Xi protests make waves outside of White House 

Despite the limited opportunities for the press to ask questions, protesters outside the White House succeeded in having Xi hear their chants for a free Hong Kong and a free Tibet.

Outside Xi’s hotel and along his driving route, signs included Xi’s face with “END CCP!” written across the bottom. Another featured a picture of Trump underneath an umbrella with “communism has no place in America” written in white.

Protesters were gathered along a fence outside of Lafayette Park and could be heard from the White House’s North Portico as Xi made his arrival for the state dinner.

The demonstrators shouted that Xi was not welcome in the U.S., and advocated on several issues, including freedoms in Tibet and Hong Kong and keeping China out of Taiwan.

The Associated Press reported that some protesters also congregated outside the Chinese Embassy before marching through Washington.

AI is a major topic of discussion 

Trump, who has taken to calling AI “super intelligence” or SI, said Wednesday that it would be a “big topic of discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is.”

But Xi on Thursday said that the U.S. and China have an obligation to manage the development of AI as “leading nations” in the industry.

“We have both the capability and responsibility to develop and manage AI for good and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control and serves the well-being of the people,” Xi said in the White House’s Grand Foyer. 

A readout of Trump and Xi’s meeting from the Chinese said that Xi told Trump that the two countries “may have competition, but they may cooperate even more.”

“AI must be kept under human control. A people-centered approach should be upheld, and AI should be developed for the positive and for good, so that AI will serve the progress of humanity,” the readout said.

Some of AI’s biggest names were in attendance at Thursday’s state dinner, including OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and Alphabet’s Sundar Pichai.

Accusations of China aiding Iran in war loom

Trump was under scrutiny from lawmakers in both parties for the lavish visit, particularly because of accusations China has helped Iran in the war against the U.S. 

The backlash came after The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that Iranian customs data showed Chinese entities made thousands of shipments in components that have been used in drones and missiles. 

Additionally, senators were informed of growing military cooperation between Iran and China at a closed-door national security briefing on Thursday. Republican and Democratic senators, in turn, called on Trump to confront Xi on the matter. 

U.S. Ambassador to China David Perdue told CNBC in an interview that Trump raised the issue during his meeting with Xi on Thursday. 

“We made it very clear to them weeks ago that any help that they would give Iran, whether it be direct or indirect, whether it be intelligence or parts or military equipment, was totally unacceptable,” Perdue said. 

“President Trump made that very clear again yesterday,” he continued. “This is an ongoing drumbeat that we have made very clear to them.” 

Chinese press clash with White House staff

Tensions were already running high in the run up to the state visit between the U.S. press and the White House over Trump’s decision to ban three outlets from covering the White House. 

However, tensions were also running high between White House and Secret Service staffers and the Chinese press during the state visit. 

Videos shared online by journalists at the White House showed Chinese journalists appearing to refuse to move for the Secret Service on the South Lawn. The refusal of the Chinese journalists resulted in Secret Service staff physically having to move them out of the way. 

White House staff were also seen repeatedly trying to keep Chinese journalists out of the camera shots of other journalists during the Rose Garden military review. 

This is not the first time Chinese reporters have clashed with U.S. staff. The New York Post reported that a Chinese journalist trampled a White House aide during Trump’s visit to Beijing in May.

data.title: Anti-Trump attorney: 'Don't overreact' to Supreme Court voter database decision
data.description:
Norm Eisen, a former White House ethics lawyer and frequent critic of President Trump, urged Americans not to “overreact” after the Supreme Court’s Friday ruling permitting the administration to move forward with its new immigration database ahead of the midterm elections. 

In an emergency ruling, the high court found that the Trump administration could proceed with its plans to allow states to use this overhauled online system to search for ineligible voters. 

Eisen noted that the majority opinion acknowledged the provision of the National Voter Registration Act that bars states from implementing systemic voter removal programs within 90 days of an election.

However, the justices noted that limited “individualized inquiries” could still proceed. 

“Page 6 of the decision makes clear that we are in the 90 day statutory window when mass changes can’t be made to voter lists!” Eisen wrote on social media. “It’s a s— decision for the reasons the 3 dissenters say but we can deal w/it.”

The decision, which was unsigned and did not provide a vote count, was opposed by the court’s three liberal justices. It overturns a lower-court ruling that prevented the Trump administration from distributing this new system to states. 

“The order below prevents the Federal Government from using the program it believes is best suited to the task,” the court wrote in its majority opinion.  

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson authored the 12-page dissenting opinion, joined by Justices Elena Kagan and Sonia Sotomayor. 

“In my view, however, the harm caused by burdening or disenfranchising even a few lawful voters outweighs the nonexistent harm that the Government experiences when it is prevented from taking an action that it likely lacks the authority to take,” Jackson wrote.

data.title: New Jersey lieutenant governor resigns after being called out by Sherrill over ethics report
data.description:
New Jersey Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell (D) resigned Friday following calls to step down from his position after an investigation found that he had violated state ethics and harassment policies.

“He submitted his resignation to me this afternoon, which I accepted,” Gov. Mikie Sherrill announced during a Friday press conference.

Sherrill called for his resignation on Thursday after releasing a 61-page ethics report detailing the findings of an independent investigation into his conduct, which included alleged sexual harassment and violating the state’s workplace discrimination policy.

According to the firm hired by the state to conduct the probe, investigators said they found credible evidence that Caldwell’s behavior violated workplace policy.

Caldwell allegedly made a sexually charged comment to a staffer and twice attempted to secure a promotion for a state employee with whom he had a romantic relationship.

Investigators also found he brought personal guests to ticketed events without paying for their admission or reimbursing the cost.

Sherrill gave Caldwell until Friday to resign from his position, saying he had “engaged in serious, repeated violations of state policy and failed to uphold the responsibilities of his office.”

“The Lieutenant Governor’s resignation is necessary and in the best interest of New Jersey residents,” she said.

Among the incidents detailed in the report, investigators said Caldwell made a romantic advance toward the female friend of a staffer. After the woman rejected him, Caldwell allegedly told the staffer, “You young women are looking for young sperm.”

Caldwell, who also oversees the state’s elections as secretary of state, denied making the remark, but investigators said they did not find his denial credible.

His attorney, Thomas Calcagni, disputed the investigation’s findings Thursday, arguing that the process was one-sided and did not give Caldwell a sufficient opportunity to respond to the allegations.

Sherrill announced Friday that acting state Comptroller Shirley Emehelu will take over as acting secretary of state, just weeks before the midterm election.

With the lieutenant governor’s office now vacant, under New Jersey’s succession rules, the state Senate president — in this case,  state Sen. Nicholas Scutari (D) — is next in line to assume the governor’s duties when Sherill is out of state or otherwise unable to serve.

data.title: Costco is offering $60 shop cards to qualifying members: How it works
data.description:
(NEXSTAR) – Costco shoppers, it’s time to check those receipts.

The popular warehouse store is offering rebates for members who spent money in the past month on dozens of popular brands owned by Procter & Gamble.

The qualifying purchases include products in the following Costco categories: Family + Home, Fabric, Beauty and Health.

If you spent $200 on those items (brands listed below), you qualify for a $60 in-store shop card. Purchases totaling $100 are good for a $25 rebate.

If your Costco receipts usually wind up in a trash can somewhere between the store exit and the food court, you can still take advantage of the deal.

To find your old receipts, sign in at Costco.com, click “Account,” “Orders and Purchases” and then select the “Warehouse” tab.

According to Costco, the original purchase dates must have been between Aug. 24, 2026 and Sept. 20, 2026, and receipts must be submitted online or postmarked by Oct. 31, 2026.

Brands included in the offer are: Align, Always, Bounce, Bounty, Cascade, Charmin, Crest, Dawn, Downy, Febreze, Gain, Gillette, Head & Shoulders, Mielle, Metamucil, Mr. Clean, Native, Olay, Old Spice, Oral-B, Pampers, Pantene, Pepto-Bismol, Prilosec, Secret, Spruce, Super Nature, Swiffer, Tampax, Tide, Venus, Vicks, Zevo.

According to the rules, items that cost more than $80 and products from Braun and SK-II are not eligible. Complete rules can be found on the Costco website.

data.title: McConnell, Cornyn join letter questioning Trump invite to Putin
data.description:
A group of senators, including seven Republicans, sent an open letter to President Trump on Friday to express “serious concern” and press Trump to explain why he invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to attend the G20 Leaders’ Summit in Miami later this year amid Russia’s war with Ukraine. 

“Given President Putin’s continued actions against the Ukrainian people and U.S. national security interests, we urge you to reconsider granting President Putin the stature and legitimacy to appear in the United States as a world leader at the G20 Leaders’ Summit,” the senators wrote. 

Such a letter is common from Democrats, in this case the opposite party to the president. But the handful of Republicans who signed on went beyond the usual Trump critics in the GOP: Sens. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.), John Cornyn (R-Texas), Roger Wicker (R-Miss.), Jerry Moran (R-Kan.), Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), John Curtis (R-Utah) and Alan Armstrong (R-Okla.). 

Their support for the letter, which urged Trump to rescind any such invitation to Putin and any other sanctioned Russian officials, demonstrates how Senate Republicans generally still support Ukraine in its war with Russia and some have become more willing to push back on Trump amid his low approval rating. 

The letter also cited the recently passed Russia-Iran sanctions bill, named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), who was one of the staunchest defenders of Ukraine in the Senate before his death in July. That bill increased sanctions on Russia, hoping to squeeze it economically as its aggression in Ukraine continues four years after invading that country. 

But Russian officials have still been present at official meetings around the U.S. in recent months, the senators said, even those who are already sanctioned. 

“It is troubling that, despite being sanctioned, these individuals have been given access to participate in G20 forums hosted in the United States,” the senators wrote. “The G20 is intended to foster international cooperation on critical issues including finance, trade and global economic stability. As Russia continues its war against Ukraine and refuses to agree to a just and lasting peace agreement, its government should not be afforded a business-as-usual treatment alongside other nations at G20 events.” 

Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and Wicker, the chair of the Senate Armed Services Committee, sent a similar letter to administration officials in April questioning Russian delegates’ participation in meetings with members of Congress and executive branch officials. 

The G20 Leaders’ Summit is an annual gathering of 19 sovereign nations’ representatives from across the world. The countries together represent 85 percent of gross world product and over half of the world’s population. 

Trump is hosting it in December at his resort in Miami.

data.title: Bill Clinton: 'There were lots of times when I wanted to ban the White House press corps'
data.description:
Former President Bill Clinton rebuked President Trump’s attempted ban of three outlets from the White House earlier this week, saying during his presidency “there were lots of times when I wanted to ban the White House press corps.”

“I got news for the people who work in the White House today. There were lots of times when I wanted to ban the White House press corps,” he said at the Clinton Global Initiative 2026 summit. “And there’s a reason we have a constitution. Because none of us are immune from being pissed off.”

“But I’m glad I never did and I’m glad I couldn’t. And these people shouldn’t. The law should be what it is,” the former president added.

His wife, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, called the ban against the three outlets “deeply disturbing,” in a Tuesday interview with The Washington Post.

“That is part of the give-and-take in not just politics, but democracy,” she said, continuing that such a ban is “unfortunately what authoritarians do.”

On Thursday, a judge ruled in favor of CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, ordering the White House to reverse its ban. Journalists from the three outlets were initially denied entry into the White House following the court’s ruling but were given access later in the day. 

MS NOW and CNN journalists also reported on Thursday that they were denied access to the state dinner arrival at the White House during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the U.S., which was a pre-credentialed event. 

Former President Barack Obama has also weighed in on the controversy, stating at an event Monday night that he believed this issue “should not be a partisan issue” as this “should be something that rises above partisanship.”

Obama said he was not surprised by the ban and it was as if “the president of the United States can’t take some criticism,” according to CNN.

“You do not have, as far as I can tell, any substantial group of Republicans who are standing up and saying, ‘No, you can’t do that, because we don’t want, if there’s a Democratic president, to be banning Fox News,’ or whatever other outlets that are going off on Democratic presidents,” he said.

data.title: Live updates: Xi departs after 3-day Trump visit; Iran war, economic squeeze weigh on GOP
data.description:
President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping wrapped up their three-day summit in Washington on Friday, as some GOP lawmakers bristle at the lavish treatment China’s prime minister received while the nation grapples with economic pressures.

The leaders’ meeting at the White House on Thursday touched on trade, artificial intelligence and the war in Iran. Trump also showed his Chinese counterpart around the White House grounds, including his new helipad and ballroom construction. They met one last time on Friday for a visit to the National Archives before Xi left for China later that afternoon.

After the Chinese prime minister’s departure, Trump wrote in a Truth Social post that he plans to meet with Xi two more times this year — in China in November for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting, as well as in December during the Group of 20 Summit in Miami. 

Meanwhile, Senate Republicans on Thursday blocked another war powers resolution seeking to end Trump’s military operations in Iran. Rising gas prices tied to the conflict and increased bond yields are squeezing the economy ahead of November. Insiders can read more here from The Hill’s Niall Stanage.

Plus, the five major television networks were back in the White House television pool on Friday following their standoff with the president over CNN’s access to the campus. Their return comes a day after a federal judge ordered the Trump administration to restore CNN, MS NOW and Politico’s access to White House grounds.

After the ruling, reporters were able to return to the White House Thursday, but the TV pool held out with its boycott — unsure if CNN broadcasters would also be allowed back to the campus. Later in the day, Trump lashed out at the networks for not covering his summit with Xi.

The president will hold executive time and policy meetings throughout the day. He also has signing time scheduled for 4:30 p.m. EDT.

Follow live below.

data.title: Huckabee points to 3 factors in many Americans turning against Israel
data.description:
U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee laid out multiple reasons why Americans may be turning against Israel in an interview Thursday — the same day Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu defended the country’s actions at the United Nations General Assembly.

Huckabee pointed to social media disinformation and foreign propaganda, a lack of “biblical literacy” and a hatred toward people who accept that “there is a God and that he’s made up the rules for life” are to blame for Americans’ rising dissatisfaction towards Israel. 

“You add all that together, I guess you just want to be mad at Israel and blame them for everything,” Huckabee said during a discussion with NewsNation’s Leland Vittert.

“And it’s very unfortunate because Israel has actually given to the world and especially to America and our partnership some very valuable things,” he added.

According to Pew Research Center survey, favorable views of the Israeli government have dropped in recent years, with 62 percent of Americans holding an unfavorable view of nation’s government. A wide partisan gap has appeared as well, with 51 percent of Republicans holding favorable opinions of the Netanyahu-led government while only 16 percent of Democrats feel the same. Americans also have low confidence in Netanyahu himself.

While Democrats have more widely criticized Israel in recent years, Republicans have also changed their tone on the Middle Eastern ally, particularly since the start of the Iran war early this year, which was launched in tandem with Israel.

Former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-Ga.) called Israeli actions in Gaza a genocide, while conservative commentator Tucker Carlson has been critical of both the Gaza war and Israel’s role in pushing the U.S. into Iran. Carlson travelled to Israel for a tense interview with Huckabee in February.

They Greene and Carlson are both part of a small but loud segment of Trump’s MAGA coalition that says the president has broken his promise to stay out of foreign wars and put “America first.”

Danny Danon, Israel’s ambassador to the U.N., disputed the falling statistics in an interview this week, blaming the way the questions were asked for the low scores. Danon told The Hill that he believes the majority of Americans “appreciate the bond and alliance between the people” of the U.S. and Israel.

Huckabee has been criticized by figures including Rep. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) for claiming Israel has a biblical claim to land beyond its current borders, and that it would “be fine” if Israel expanded across the region along with actions.

“He’s become a complete apologist for the most extreme Israeli government in history,” Van Hollen said. “He should be defending Americans and defending American interests, he’s failed to do so.”

Huckabee argued claims that Israeli actions in Gaza were genocidal or that it is an apartheid state are wrong and that people will have to be willing to “look at truth” to start to improve American views of the nation.

“This is a place where Muslims, Druze, Christians serve in the military. They vote. They can be in the Knesset. Quite a few Arabs are in the Knesset,” Huckabee said. “They serve on the Supreme Court. They run some of the biggest businesses in the country. If you’re apartheid, that’s not making any sense.”

“I think it’s somewhat of a spiritual problem where people just don’t want to hear the truth because they want to be mad at somebody,” Huckabee said. “Well, let’s pick on the Jews.”

data.title: Senate approves legislation targeted at pilot, air traffic control mental health guidance
data.description:
The Senate passed two bills Thursday aimed at removing barriers for pilots and air traffic controllers seeking mental health treatment, as well as reduce stigma surrounding these conditions.

Sponsored by Sens. John Hoeven (R-N.D.) and Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), respectively, both pieces of legislation passed in the upper chamber by unanimous consent. 

The first act, which Hoeven introduced, would require the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to issue guidance encouraging pilots and air traffic controllers struggling with mental health issues to seek treatment. It would also provide “enhanced” training for aviation medical examiners on how to address these conditions. 

The bill honors John A. Hauser, an aviation student from Chicago who took his own life in 2021 while attending the University of North Dakota.

“Our nation faces a severe shortage of qualified pilots and air traffic controllers, while bureaucratic delays and outdated processes at the FAA keep these professionals from working for prolonged periods when they seek mental health care,” Hoeven said in a statement after senators passed the package.

The other bill, brought forth by Duckworth, seeks to boost transparency around available medications for aviation industry employees.

This legislation, titled the “Aviation Medication Transparency Act of 2026,” would direct the FAA to create and annually update a list of medications that can be safely prescribed to pilots and air traffic controllers. 

“Our aviation system depends on the well-being of our pilots and air traffic controllers, who operate under an immense amount of stress,” Duckworth said in a statement. “Their careers should never be threatened because they weren’t properly informed about which medications they’re allowed to take, or simply sought the mental health care they need.”  

Both bills now head to the House for consideration. 

Earlier this year, the FAA issued new guidance encouraging pilots and air traffic controllers to seek counseling, as well as other mental health services. The Hill has reached out to the agency for comment on the Senate’s approval of these two bills.
